This past summer, I worked as a software engineer intern (backend/cloud infrastructure) and had the opportunity to implement a feature that gave clients much more flexibility and control over their virtual machines (which they purchased and are hosted in the company servers). 

Basically my project was to modify an API so that clients can seamlessly change the # of cores and amount of memory in GBs that their virtual machines used up! The original process was manual and took many hours before I started working this job, and by the time I left, I got the functionality to work in a little under 60 seconds. I implemented this feature in Java, and I'm really proud of this project because I got to work with other software engineers, a technical PM, a high-level PM, and a UX designer - all for the code I was writing in those short 3 months. 

Some challenges I faced were adjusting to a ginormous codebase of existing production code / reading previous engineers' (sometimes messy) code, when I couldn't grab a server host for my team-wide demo presentation in time due to service issues, and when my high-level PM left for maternity leave so I had to finish my project 2 weeks early. I think that all of these challenges made me a better engineer by the end of my experience, and it's helped me become a smarter, more communicative, and honest team member in any given situation.

Just this summer, I got into making spreadsheets for different data sets, and taught myself how to use Apps Scripts on Google Sheets, which is basically a way to implement JavaScript into your Google Sheet in order to do more complicated functions. 

My favorite sheet that I made was a sort of “mock SIS,” in which I created a database with around 500 courses that are currently in SIS (including information about what attributes they have, number of credits, typical semesters run, etc.). Then, in various different tabs, I programmed a way to create a new schedule or upload an old one, see if that schedule fulfills my major and minor requirements, and store that schedule for later use! 

To build the project, I started off quite simply, trying to do as much of the code as I could with the provided functions within Google Sheets. As I did, I made a list of functions I could not make, and then proceeded to program those ones using Apps Scripts. Finally, I made the sheets aesthetically pleasing and added conditional formatting!

The most challenging part of this project was definitely the code itself. I was still relatively new to JavaScript and Apps Scripts when I began this project, so I pretty much taught myself as I went. Another challenging – and less expected – issue I ran into was the efficiency of my code. Because there ended up being so many tabs in the spreadsheet and so many functions, I often found that my code was running too slowly so I needed to find ways to make it simpler.

If you want to check it out, here’s the link to the project (you may be prompted with an “authorization required” popup if pressing buttons or editing certain tabs – that’s just for the Apps Scripts!): https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1azAhfeZmhdMANRSj-0eMV8Nsd9_2zn7WQ7bgPf_Y8gA/edit?usp=sharing

In doing so, the non-profit is granting women the ability to break the cycle, and maybe one day, to have enough money to no longer live in poverty. I would also love to work for this group because the web app seems really cool, and I would love to see it come together first-hand!

Over the past summer, I worked as a frontend engineer at a Boston-based design firm. The firm focused on building and rebranding websites for higher education institutions and I was able to work on a variety of projects. 

One project I spent a majority of my time on was for VCU Art's campus in Qatar. This project really excited me because there is a lot of interaction and animations on the website that made it very visually engaging. In the earlier stages of the project, I worked with designers to understand what techniques they used to create the best visual system to engage the specific audience for an arts school. The bold and eccentric images and color palettes spoke to the brand and resulted in a very interesting website. I developed it using mostly HTML/CSS and Javascript, and a variety of tools like sass and php for optimal organization. This is a wordpress website that isn't launched yet, but I have linked it below. One major challenge when implementing this site is that there were a lot of high resolution images and the other developers and I needed to figure out a way to allow the page to load quickly enough to engage the audience while delivering high quality images. Further, since so much of the site is visual and not words, there were concerns regarding screen readers being able to fully communicate the message to those who use special tools. column15: A project I am proud of is a personal project I made called Theta Budget Tracker. In my sorority, Kappa Alpha Theta, at Tufts, I am in charge of the budget. Currently, the way the budget website works is that I am the only one who has access to the budget. In turn, other members of the executive board have to text me to find out their remaining budget and I have to be near my computer to find an answer for them. In order to alleviate this problem, I created the Theta Budget Tracker using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Jquery, Selenium WebDriver, Python, and Heroku. The user of the website has to select a specific part of the budget they would like to view. Then, they click the search button. On the backend, the website uses Selenium and Python to log into my VP of Finance account, navigate to the budget page, load the budget, find the specific budget request, and then return the overall budget and current budget for that section. Once this data is found, some simple subtraction is performed to determine the amount of money spent so far. The overall budget, the current budget, and the amount of money spent for this section are then displayed in a table. The user can then ask to display another section of the budget. The above process will repeat and the data will be added to another row of the table. The one big challenge I faced was learning how to deploy it on Heroku. Through countless hours of research, I finally figured it out! I then showed the final project to the executive board and they really liked it! They felt it did streamline the process of keeping track of their remaining budget.

I'm proud of this color sensor game that I recreated off of a Facebook post this past summer during my internship. Using SPIKE Prime, the premise of the game was that a random color would display on the hub and the user would have a set amount of time to turn 4 bricks (green, blue, red, and yellow) to match the displayed color. Each time the user got it correct, the time they have for their next turn decreases, but if they got it wrong, the game would end. 

I referenced the model on Facebook, but had to consider how to build the spinning feature so that it would happen smoothly. Once it was satisfactory, I coded it in word blocks (similar to Scratch). One challenge was that the code was initially long and repetitive because I had a large if-else if loop that would check on each turn. My manager preferred code that was shorter and cleaner, so I toyed with lists and created my own variables. Another challenge came when I then translated that code into Micropython, which was compatible with the SPIKE Prime hub, because I wasn't sure what the syntax looked like. I discovered that there was a feature where I could pick directly from a list, which helped make the code cleaner. Since I already had a form of the code as word blocks, it was relatively straight forward to adapt that into Micropython. It was really fun to play the game when I finished it and hear the sound effects that I put in.

OO I really like this question. Last year, I made an anagrams discord bot which basically simulates the iOS Game Pigeon game "Anagrams" if you've ever played that. It works exactly like the actual game which basically gives you a bunch of letters and allows you 60 seconds to tap the letters to create words.
Say you were given, 'A, T, R, E, C, S' you would tap the letters to make words such as "caters," "traces," "reacts," "crates," "races," etc. The longer the word, the more points it gives you.
For this project I coded the bot in Python and used the Discord API and I made it so that it could handle multiple user-inputted commands to carry out different variations of the game.
List of commands:
*anagrams 6
Plays anagrams with a random 6-letter word
*anagrams 7
Plays anagrams with a random 7-letter word
*anagrams <word>
Plays anagrams with a given word
I also gave the game a 60-second timer so that once the time runs out, it shows you your score, the words you got, and all the words you missed.

During my senior year of high school, our STEM club joined a county competition where the objective was to build a chain-reaction contraption that fit the annual theme for that year (I think, for my year, it was "Flip a Page"). Our club decided to take the telling-a-tale route, but rather than telling a fictional tale, we wanted our contraption to traverse through different periods, encapsulating memorable events in history. We were also aiming for the 'Most Green' award, so our project was primarily constructed out of recyclable materials and miscellaneous objects donated by our local businesses/organizations.

We went through a couple of weeks of design and concept brainstorming. Then, teams were formed for each era, and we would work on our individual ideas in our sections before coming together to consolidate how to connect each section together. My team documented the Mesozoic and Prehistoric Eras, and we tried to incorporate simple mechanics like pulleys and levers using string and cardboard (I also made a cardboard dinosaur!). 

One of the challenges was the communication and organization of our project. Sometimes, some teams would fall behind schedule, and other times, the plans for a particular section of the contraption would not be fully flushed out, so we would jump around from team to team, trying our best to help. Furthermore, due to clashing schedules (both classwork and other extracurriculars), we could not put forth consistent hours working on this project. But, despite all the challenges, we did walk away with a completed Rube Goldberg contraption that worked and many cool photos from the event! I know this was not a coding project, which I hope was okay, but I think I am pretty proud of it, given our complications. It also gave me a taste of the design process and a deep appreciation to coordinators of well-organized projects.

Each year throughout high school I participated in the “Arc” community engagement program, where students met with people from the local Merrimack Valley area with cognitive disabilities. As a freshman, my buddy Ted and I spent our time listening to music and folding paper. Although Ted was unable to communicate verbally, I learned how to read Ted’s facial expressions and body language. As a sophomore, my buddy Jeff and I walked and talked. I found what comforted Jeff most was being a sounding board to allow him to process certain situations, like his sleep apnea and his mother’s health. I was selected to be a coordinator of the program my junior year and in August 2020, I was notified that Arc would be canceled due to the pandemic. I proposed to our faculty advisors that instead of canceling the program, students write weekly letters to their buddies to stay connected and keep Arc alive. My suggestion was embraced, and “Arc Pals” was born. All of our Arc students met remotely each week to share stories and write to our buddies. Throughout the 2020-2021 school year, we heard that buddies were truly enjoying the letters and some even responded with their own letters, maintaining the love that is always so tangible at Arc.

I also volunteered at Senior Connections, a subset of Andover Elder Services where many of the participants had memory difficulties, for four years in high school. During my time there, I became close with many of the members and learned a lot about their stories (like Lucinda - a wedding photographer in New York in the sixties who loved to bring in photos that she took to show everyone - and Tom - often a quiet man, but was always the loudest in the room when 1960s hits were playing). I really felt like I had sixteen grandparents whenever I was at Senior Connections (they even offered me their cookies and crackers during snack time)! During 2020, when I couldn’t physically volunteer at the Robb Center, I filmed, edited, and published bingo and trivia videos for the group to play so I could still be with them virtually. It was truly a blast getting to know the entire Senior Connections group and I loved hearing all the stories that they told with a smile on their faces as they reminisced.

This past summer, I worked at APCC (Association to Preserve Cape Cod), a non-profit organization focused on protecting and preserving the natural beauty of the Cape. I was a Cyanobacteria Monitoring Intern, collecting freshwater pond samples and testing for cyanobacteria. Cyanobacteria is a toxin-producing bacteria found in freshwater bodies of water that can cause skin irritation, liver damage, pet deaths, and possibly more severe ailments. Not only did I learn a lot about cyanobacteria and the geography of the cape, but I gained a great respect for the natural beauty of the Cape (and all places that we call home, for that matter). I also had first-hand experience with negative human interactions in local ecology through fertilizers and pesticides. It was a very rewarding experience to be able to see my work translating to a safer living environment for the inhabitants and visitors of Cape Cod.

I’m a huge golfer. That’s not to say that I’m very good at the game but I love playing and I’m addicted to improving. I watched a lot of PGA events towards the end of summer and became very intrigued with Trackman technology and how it created a shot tracer of the ball, making me want to create my own at-home version with putting. Using YOLOv8 from Ultralytics and the OpenCV library, I created an object detection program for golf putting. Given a video of a putt, the program tracks the ball and hole locations and determines whether the ball went in the hole or not. If the ball goes in, the program spits out important information about the putt, such as the angle taken between the straight line path from the ball to the hole and the initial line of the actual putt (where the person hit it), the total amount of break (how far the putt moved due to the topography of the green, in pixels), and the total distance of the ball from the hole (also in pixels). It also draws a line from the ball to the hole and puts dots at every location of the ball throughout the video to make a tracer. 

I wrote this program in Python and it was a blast, but there were a bunch of difficulties that I had along the way. One of the first difficulties that I had was very early on in the project. I initially tried to download a pre-made data set for training the object detection model, but that introduced a lot of problems. Firstly, the data set didn’t include any pictures of golf holes. So, I grabbed photos from the internet, took screenshots from YouTube accounts like PGA, Good Good, and Bob Does Sports, and snapped photos at my local course. However, even after expanding the data set a lot, my model really struggled to track the ball when it was close to the hole. I realized this must be because of how I labeled photos using Roboflow. I used the rectangular shape to label golf balls and holes, but occasionally when I would label photos of a golf ball actually going into the hole, these rectangles would overlap and I figured that must really “confuse” the model. So, I took a few hours one night and manually outlined hundreds of photos with golf balls and holes (I drew outlines around all of the objects to be as precise as possible) to label them in Roboflow. Then I retrained the model and it worked much better. But even after I solved that problem, I had difficulties determining and implementing the code for a successful putt. A putt isn’t necessarily made if the ball reaches the hole or if it is “on line.” What if a putt looks like it’s about to go in, then it lips out (rides the rim of the golf hole but somehow still misses)? What about a putt that is about to go in, but then stops just short of the hole? Or a putt that ends up directly on the other side of the hole due to a lot of break in the green or a lip out? I eventually decided to use the confidence of the object detection to tell whether the ball had actually gone in the hole or not. Each tracking point has an associated confidence level (between 0 and 1, with the higher being more confident) and I decided - after some trial - that if the ball was within the vicinity of the hole (~ 10 pixels) and the confidence level dropped below 0.4, it could be assumed that the ball had gone in. Of course, this isn’t 100 percent accurate, but the cases in which it won’t work are relatively few and far between. 

I’m really proud of this project because it combined my programming knowledge and something that I really love to do and it was a self-motivated project that actually worked out in the end and was really fun to make!
column29:
I am very interested in The Legacy Project because its values align closely with mine and its mission hits very close to home with me. Having spent four years volunteering at Senior Connections, I understand first-hand how important memories are to seniors. If we weren’t playing bingo, trivia, or a different game, I was often listening to the incredible stories that the seniors had. I was particularly close to one member of the group, Duane, one of the older members who had Parkinson’s. I cannot explain the difference in his expressions between when he was sitting down with the group playing a game and talking about his life. A young, successful CEO, Duane was an avid car collector back in his day who still drove his precious Mustang to Senior Connections on the days he felt well enough to do so. I won’t ever forget how his face lit up as he gave me career advice based on his work experience or how his legs swayed to Beatles music as we reminisced on the music from his generation. However, many of these accounts are never written down. I would never know about Lucinda’s photography career and how many presidents she met if it weren’t for meeting her in person.

One exception to this case is my grandmother (who we call Nonni). Nonni has had quite the exciting life. Growing up as the child of Italian immigrants, my grandmother is one of four children. Her brother Anthony had Down syndrome and passed away when I was very young. Her sister Ro passed away due to a brain tumor before she was only thirty years old. Her other brother Pat passed away before he was sixty as the result of a heart attack. So, I never really met any of my grandmother’s siblings. But I still feel like I know them. Not only has Nonni told me countless stories about their rambunctious household as children, but she wrote a book about her life called “It’s All About Me,” which I have in my bedroom at home. This book tells the story of Nonni’s life, from her childhood in Massachusetts, teaching on a military base in Japan where she met my grandfather (who we called Dibi) and got married, traveling across Europe, giving birth to my Uncle in Italy, and eventually settling back in Easton, Massachusetts. I can’t possibly share a tenth of the details and intricacies of Nonni’s stories, but I hope you understand it has been an amazing ride, as she reminds us often. This book is not just an amazing read for me to see my grandmother’s life story, absorb many of the lessons she learned along the way, and hear the many voices of relatives that I never met. “It’s All About Me” also helps me remember my grandfather’s legacy - who is no longer with us - and will always be a living artifact of my grandmother’s legacy. I know that I will be able to give this book to my children many years from now and they will be able to understand who we are as a family and appreciate Nonni and Dibi’s legacies. I will also always be able to go back to this book when I need inspiration for a life adventure from my grandparents.

Therefore, I understand and appreciate the stories and legacies of seniors and would be honored to help The Legacy Mission in their pursuit of sharing and recording their life experiences, because I know that we are a sliver of ourselves without the lives and stories of those who came before us.



The Emerald Necklace Conservancy also really jumped out to me at the GIM, not only because of Roger and Ben’s enthusiasm (although I must say, that was awesome), but because this past summer working at APCC has really shown me the importance of the preservation of our local nature. Not only did I develop a deeper appreciation for the specific ecosystems near ponds by walking through wooded areas on the way to obscure pond locations to sample water, but I began to understand - on a small scale - just how much harm humans are causing in these areas. I saw countless warning signs posted at ponds due to elevated concentrations of cyanobacteria and one post in our weekly newsletter from the director of APCC resonated heavily with me (many of these cyanobacteria “blooms” are caused by fertilizer and pesticide runoff). He wrote about having to tell his young nephew/niece that they could not swim in the pond at his house this year because of cyanobacteria. The child was devastated because they only get to visit the Cape once a summer and couldn’t even go in the water at their uncle’s house. I used to visit my relative’s house in Onset, Massachusetts every year when I was younger and it was the week that I looked forward to most in the summer. I cannot imagine how upset I would have been if I could not go in the water. This is just a small anecdote to a much larger problem that we are seeing on the Cape, in Massachusetts, and in the world. Our use of chemicals (in the case of cyanobacteria: fertilizers and pesticides) and pure ignorance regarding the environment are causing us to lose many of the naturally beautiful aspects of the world. It hurts to see that happening in the Cape and it hurts equally as much to see it happen in the Boston area. Therefore, the Emerald Necklace Conservancy’s mission to restore and protect the 1100 acres of “Boston’s best outdoor space” is one that I would love to support through JumboCode.

Our game's premise ended up being that a player would collect letters as they appeared and moved on a track in front of the player. My other teammate and I used the Godot game engine to organize the game into scenes and to implement the game mechanics. The first challenge I faced while participating in this project is that I had never coded a video game before or used Godot. There was definitely a learning curve for me while creating the game. I decided to create a Moroccan Arabic Wordle game because I was playing the wordle in English, French, and Spanish everyday. This project was not typical, as Wordle is not well-known in Morocco. However, I was excited to forge a new way to promote Moroccan Arabic culture and language learning, especially in areas heavily dominated by French culture.

I implemented the game using the Pygame library and Python, which were pretty easy to use. The game was a daily interactive experience that encouraged people in my highschool to explore the Moroccan Arabic dialect. 

One of the biggest challenges I am still facing is that there is no dictionary of all Moroccan Arabic words, so the game is unable to check whether a word exists or not. As a result, players can input random letters and still be able to enter a word. I don’t think it is an issue I will ever be able to solve, but the game is still fun as it is!

I am proud of this project because it allowed me to use my skills to promote Moroccan culture and language learning. I really love how here in the US, the motto is more learning by doing rather than learning by studying, and that definitely pushed me to make this project.

A project that really piqued my interest came during my 10- week bootcamp with Veritas AI. For our final capstone project, we built an AI model to predict NBA's regular season MVP using matchup data collected over 2 seasons. We chose to build a logistic regression model to assign weights to particular statistics, and awarded an MVP point to a player if his predicted win probability based on his stats was greater than the average win probability. Players were then ranked in descending order of MVP points- and our predicted MVP for 2021-22 season was actually correct! 

Initially, we started off with a basic model which produced a mere 53% accuracy, but as we fine tuned the program and incorporated logistic regression- our predictive model went up to 57% accuracy. A project I'm proud of (albeit incomplete) is a demo version for a trash collecting robot I've been developing for some years now. I started this project because I believe there is value in the waste that we produce due to our highly consumeristic tendancies. I wanted to try and capture the trash thrown into our waste stream via this robot in the hopes of being able to convert into something that isn't a net negative to our environment through recyling, composting, etc.

The demo, in essense, is a cup detection robot that's suppose to classify red cups from blue cups. It's suppose to serve as a proof of concept for the large project at hand. It utilizes object detection (ML), computer vision, and stereovision so the learning curve when I started this out as a high schooler was pretty steep. I started out by build a proper PC to train different models on the hundreds of images I had taken of red cups and blue cups. For a while after that, I was tweaking the model so that it would yield the best inference results. When I got to a point where I was satisfied with its inferences, I moved on to work on how to take in a video stream through two cameras and run inferences from both streams of data. In addition to this, for the robot to be able to truly work out the object's spacial positioning e.i. how far it is from the robot, I needed to implement stereovision. Currently, what's next on the robot roadmap is to figure out how to port my model to a smaller computer such as a Raspi since I've been doing most of my testing on my desktop.

The largest challenge I've faced when working on this project was figuring out how to implement stereovision in the program. Sterovision is a very linear algebra heavy topic and, generally speaking, figuring out an object's 3D spacial position from 2D images is hard task. Learning the mathematical apparatus for this and implementing it in code (even though I was using a framework) proved to be quite the challenge.

One project I am proud of is the program I developed during my internship this summer at Verint. I worked on the Forecasting & Scheduling team and the purpose of my program was to help engineers on the team more easily debug scheduler runs. The program was triggered every time there was a failed scheduler run. It compressed the generated logs folder, and uploaded that folder to a centralized AWS S3 bucket where the folder could be accessed easily. 

Initially, to implement this program, I developed a Java program that would be built into the scheduler itself and would trigger every time a scheduler run failed. However, after discussing with my manager, it was decided the the program would be implemented using current Verint framework and a YAML program. Now, there would be a Datadog monitor, that would monitor scheduler runs and execute the YAML program once the monitor was triggered.

There were two main challenges I faced when developing this program. The first was that neither me or my manager had much experience with YAML or the framework I would have to integrate the program into. I had to learn much of it on my own and then explain to my manager the current state of the program and how it worked each time we met. The second challenge was integrating the program into the existing framework. I had to use Rundeck and Terraform, both of which I had not used before, in order to integrate my script into the framework and allow it to be triggered properly with the right information. Many changes had to be made to successfully integrate the program. Once the program was integrated, the monitor had to be created to trigger at the right time and pass in the right information into the script. 

I learned much from this experience. Not only about new languages and frameworks, but also how to learn new material on my own and then apply it to my job. In the end, it was incredibly satisfying seeing all the parts come together and the program working in production.

I built a machine learning pipeline that identifies 4 upperlimb gym exercises during an internship at Coros Wearables last summer. 

The pipeline takes in 6 axis of Innertial Measurement Units (Acceleration and Angular velocity) and derives the current gym exercise that the user is done. 

I started by processing the input data through a number of time series processing techniques. Such as bandpass filters (I used a butterworth filter), sliding windows (for feature extraction) and visualization (for intuitive understanding). I achieved this mainly through SciPy, but I designed my own implementation of the butterworth filter.

 I then designed a modular ensemble model using mainly Sklearn and Tensorflow. I was able to design a majority voting system to decide the output of my model based on training data. In terms of splitting for training and testing, I used the leave one sample out method, which essentially means that we extrapolate our prediction on unknown users. 

After the model is implemented and trained, I converted the codebase to C for it to embedd into firmwares. I was able to present the model to the CTO of the company. 

The biggest challenge I faced throughou the process was recognizing the limits of my hardwares. My IMU data came from wrist sensors, so I was not able to detect any periodic fluctuations from the lower body during an exercise. As a result, I limited my scope to 4 upper limb gym exercises.

Next, it was hard to find the best way to display the map skin for free, as I needed to use an API key, but I did want to do it for free. column15: Last year in my data structures class, our teacher assigned us a project that takes in a postfix expression and returns the value of that expression and the expression in infix notation. I had a lot of fun with this project because it was challenging, and I went in the completely wrong direction at first. I originally thought it should be done recursively, performing the first operation then re-running the new expression through until it was done. That proved to be the wrong strategy, however, so I decided to try it iteratively, which was much easier. I was frustrated but also glad to find that I could simply store each number in a stack until I reached the first operand, then pop two from the stack and perform the calculation. Printing the infix was also difficult, but I was able to solve it a similar way after some time. I found this project satisfying and enjoyable because it essentially decoded an 'encrypted' math equation, but challenged me to think critically about what a postfix expression truly stated (i.e. how a human is able to 'decode' it) and how I could use what I knew about coding to solve that problem most efficiently. I also created what, in my opinion, was a creative way of truncating any unnecessary '0's from the output (even though it is probably not very good or efficient). The code took the double_num % (double)int_num and checked if it equaled 0. If it did, it printed out the number cast as an int. If it did not equal zero, then it checked to see if the number times ten equaled the number times ten but cast as an int. If it did, it printed out one decimal place. If it did not, it printed out the number with two decimal places. I spent a lot of time on that and I thought it was especially cool when it worked, but I am thinking now there are probably much, much easier ways to do it.

column15:
I recently worked on a research project at Carnegie Mellon University involving testing for Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs). The end goal of the project was to automate testing by creating some sort of oracle that verifies whether a given system behaves as desired. Current oracle inference techniques have either low accuracy or are infeasible in practice. Therefore, we proposed a new framework to infer oracles in the form of formal specifications (Signal Temporal Logic) directly from the execution traces of a CPS that tackles both of the challenges above with the aid of a human-in-the-loop and mutation testing. 

The biggest challenges were at the beginning. This was a very broad topic and it was hard to give it a direction. We decided to focus on improving the accuracy of current techniques instead of explainability. Later on, we needed to find a way of choosing representative traces to query the human-in-the-loop. I was stuck here because it is complex to handle traces from CPSs, but with the aid of my mentor we were able to implement a clustering algorithm to identify representative traces.

To gather data, I implemented a Python script that automatically injects predefined mutations into the code to generate "incorrect" behavior. column15: This summer, I worked on an awesome project at MIT to develop a conversational AI for combatting loneliness in older adults. The baseline for this was that it would keep track of calls and interactions online you had with friends, family etc. and saves the transcripts and summaries of the conversation for future use. This would help to jog your memory, so you can speak on past events that have now occurred, remember what you last talked about on the last call, and reach out to others that you haven't talked to in a while. The idea is to give back confidence to those with memory issues, and encourage more social interaction. The project is still going on now, currently we are sending surveys out to a senior citizen home, and getting input on what they would like to see in a product like this. As to what I did, I worked through a lot of the back end coding by making a python application. Some of the issues I ran into were, what language learning models I should use, what kind of speaker diarization pipelines I should consider, and how i would actually transcribe the files that come through. I started at a lower level where instead of starting with phone calls directly, I would input an audio file, for example mp3's. It boils down to a couple of API calls with OpenAI, sticking time stamps and transcriptions together to make it easy for the user to understand,  and showing the summarizations afterwards. I also created a front end UI to go along with the python application using javascript and react. This front end calls a flask RestAPI, being the python application I wrote. In the future, I plan on making a more fluid ui, and work on more of the aspects of encouraging socialization. After we get responses from the survey, there will be more of an understanding of what we should prioritize!

column15: For my software engineering class, we had to create a multi-threaded simulation of the Boston Subway System using Java. However, after the introduction of locks and synchronized methods, i was able to control the access of shared memory and also be able to control how the threads moved through the system. At the start of the project, I was not passing a lot of tests, which got me worried, but at the end of the project, i was able to pass all the tests except for 3, which made me very happy. This was the longest, hardest and most strenuous project that I've ever been part of within computer science, but I was happy to come out of this with good results.

column15: The most recent project that I'm proud of was the first homework for CS40, filesofpix. Fortunately for me and my partner, Cooper, we had come up with a game plan to tackle this behemoth of an assignment as stress-free as you could possible get in CS40. We broke down each of our program's functionality into the "goal of the day" over the span of the project's lifetime. We coded, tested, and debug while making use of various resources to learn C or fix a bug. While we did have moment were it seemed like all hope was lost, we took breaks at those times and came back stronger than ever to tackle the issues in our code. By the end of the project we were uncorrupting pgm image files like it was nobody's business! We had successfully completed the first project for, arguably, the most notorious CS class offered at Tufts. Over the summer I interned at Booz Allen Hamilton. There, I created a browser application that took in various streams of real-time airplane location data displayed it on a map, and calculated real-time statistics on various regions.

I built the application with SvelteKit and type. It was mostly just a front-end application that would connect to various APIs (however I used SvelteKit to create some proxies to avoid CORS issues).

This application had various functionality. You could create a region either freehand, with a point and radius, or select one of the 13 air traffic control regions. Then you would see it on a dashboard. If you click on the more info tab, you will see statistics like the plane count, average plane heading, the variance in place flow, etc. 

I also created a simple querying console that would allow the user to search and select various planes, as well as select planes by region or property. This resembled SQL, and the queries would return a set of hex identifiers.

Also, I created a track replayer that would allow you to watch the historic track of each plane. You could rewind the current time and data and the map would completely update as well as the statistics visible on the region dashboard.

Not to toot my own horn but in my opinion, the UI was pretty stylish and modern, but not Bootstrappy if you know what I mean, The functionality used a mountable window system. This means the user could rearrange each element as they pleased.

The development of this project taught me about what a software engineering job is. Each week, my bosses would give me a list of functionality to implement. I implemented each feature with organized and explicit commits (before on personal projects my commit messages were just like "asdasdasdasd").

Also, I should note that during this summer internship, I wrote another browser application that used Babylon.js to create a live 3D spatial map that displayed plane data. It used a custom mapping engine that used the Bing maps tile API.

column15:
A really cool initiative on Tufts campus is the free food e-list from the Tufts Food Rescue Collaborative— (you can subscribe to it at http://elist.tufts.edu/wws/info/freefoodattufts). However, an e-list flies a little under the radar, so many people don’t know about it.

This summer, my friend mentioned that she wanted to turn the e-list into an app called FreeBites: Tufts students would post and comment on pictures of free food opportunities on campus, receive notifications from other posts, and be able to search/filter available posts according to their needs.

At this point, I had a little experience with web apps from CS 20, but I had no clue what went into building a mobile app. I didn’t know how to pick a(proper) tech stack, I didn’t know anything about React or React Native, and my extent of experience with Node.js was a few afternoons and an all-nighter before my CS20 project was due, so it was quickly forgotten in the ensuing delirium.

As my friend worked on Figma to come up with the preliminary designs, I started to do some research on picking a tech stack. After discussing exactly what the requirements + features were in the designs, I ended up picking React Native, using a platform called Expo, styled-components for styling(in retrospect I might try Nativewind), and Node.js/MongoDB Realms for the backend.

After that, the designers went to work on UX research and UX tryouts with their prototypes, and I went to work trying to learn and set it all up in code.

The biggest technical challenge so far(we’re still early in the project) was trying to set up the routing to hook up all the different screens, as well as routing to detect authentication (actual authentication is coming later). I spent hours on the documentation trying to beat it into my brain and set up the correct file structure, and getting it to work was super rewarding.

As the school year started, we connected with the organization behind the e-list who inspired it all, Tufts Food Rescue, and TCU, who have agreed to support us! We’re also looking into expanding the team, which means we’ll have some new choices and challenges, such as onboarding and figuring out the workflow, and possibly switching to Nativewind for styling, which I think (?) might be easier for newer coders to pick up and more consistent.

In JumboCode, I hope to get the experience of working on a larger development team so I can understand the process and what a developer would expect from a tech lead, as well as getting some experience working on the backend; so far my experience working on FreeBites has been quite frontend oriented(I didn’t want to be overwhelmed learning everything at once), but I think it’s time to start dipping my toes into backend development.

Even though we’re not done yet, it’s been a rewarding project to work on; I’ve learned a lot so far and I’m super excited to see what I can do moving forward!

Near the end of this past summer, I decided I wanted to build my first side project. After searching on the internet, I settled on Minesweeper, a game I had seen my brother play and found confusing. The backend of the game was relatively straightforward; it only required some research regarding the random library for bomb placement and overall took only one or two nights. Spirits were high, I was feeling good, and then came the frontend.

I had never used a graphics library before, and just getting it onto my computer and synced up with my Makefile was genuinely infuriating. When I tell you I was struggling, I was ALL CAPS YELLING at it. Eventually, after many YouTube tutorials, I was able to get everything synchronized. After some more headaches figuring out the drawing functions, I was able to create a basic representation of the backend.

Then came all the other features. These included three levels of difficulty (8x8, 16x16, 16x30), different music for the starting and ending menus, a timer, flags (which I didn't even know existed until the end), button noises, winning and losing animations, and files to keep track of and update the best times for each difficulty. Basically, it had every feature of Google Minesweeper except for a guaranteed non-guessing board (guessing is more fun anyway).

Disclaimer: I never really thought I was going to share the code, so the modularity and style are a little worse than I'd like them to be. Also, it won't be able to run by itself as the SFML library and sounds I downloaded are not included in the files.

column15: "Ladies and gentlemen of the 3 train, it's showtime! It's showtime!" Every passenger shifts their attention away from their phones, newspapers, or conversations to witness the New York City subway system's greatest showman, except, of course, those disembarking at the next stop. Back in my sophomore year, I enrolled in a film class outside of school. For our final project, we were assigned the task of creating a documentary. I collaborated with two other individuals. After countless hours in a room adorned with a whiteboard, we conceived the project "ShowTime" – a short film that chronicled the lives of three distinct street performers. Scouring the streets of New York City in search of our subjects turned out to be surprisingly straightforward, as people were more than willing to share their stories. Our process typically began by obtaining their phone numbers and getting to know them briefly. Subsequently, we'd inquire if they were interested in a future interview. Each interview took place in the very location where they performed. For instance, we interviewed Louis Verchatta, a man bedecked in feathers, who played a traditional Peruvian flute, in front of a vibrant rainbow mural within the Times Square station underpass. Jasean Hartley and his friends, who brought a speaker onto the subway car and danced to their music, were interviewed right inside the train car itself. Lastly, Mamadou Diop, who played the drums and provided lessons on the history of his drums and culture aboard the six train, was interviewed on a bench near the train tracks at the station adjacent to his home, where he boarded the train every day. In any project, challenges are bound to arise. On one occasion, we recorded Louis for a full ten minutes before realizing that the camera wasn't even turned on. Overcoming this hurdle necessitated creativity, as we couldn't ask him to repeat his performance. Instead, we took extra b-roll and shots of him when he wasn’t speaking. Nonetheless, this was the only major hiccup, largely because of our extensive planning. We maintained a rigorous schedule, devised a comprehensive list of questions, and prepared shot lists and backup equipment for each filming session. Ultimately, our documentary turned out to be a resounding success, ranking among my all-time favorite projects. Collaborating on a team, brainstorming together to shape our project's direction, and trusting my partners played pivotal roles in its success. Given the extensive planning, filming, and editing required, it's evident that no single individual could have undertaken all these tasks alone.

During my senior year of high school, to graduate from my “major”, I had to take CS Capstone, a full year class dedicated to creating a product for a client. In groups of three to five, we were required to go through the process of product development, starting with contacting clients, producing a minimum viable product, and finally presenting our product in front of a panel of experts in the industry.

After reaching out to multiple clients, my group ultimately worked with JoAh Academy, a newly founded test prep academy that provided 5-12th extra-curricular learning services and college consulting. Our client was looking for a way to digitize their processes as they fully operated on paper, including grading and testing. They asked us to focus on three main tasks – a new home website to act as a central hub for their clients, a testing environment to simulate digital standardized exams, and facilitated communication between students and teachers. By the end of the year, my group had created a home website as well as a dashboard system for students and teachers. Teachers/Admin would be able to create short quizzes as well as longer PDF exams, send announcements to students, administer new students, and read inquiries sent from the main website. Students would be able to read announcements and take short quizzes or PDF exams. Our tech stack involved Django, SQLite, Bootstrap, and GitHub.

Because this was our group's first time building a large scale project and working heavily with web development, we struggled a lot with time management, directory organization, and even choosing a tech stack. Choosing between advanced functionality and perfect UI was super difficult. Setting realistic expectations and presenting problems to our non tech-savvy client proved to be difficult as well. Another big challenge was working with databases and learning about security, including penetration testing! Through all these problems, with trial and error, teamwork, and time, we were able to get through all these challenges and produce a super cool project.

When I was in high school, I was lucky enough to take a class called Non-linear dynamics. In this class, we explored a bunch of different concepts like fractal trees, transforming different objects, the Mandelbrot set, logistic bifurcation, and graphics. One of my favorite projects from that class was when we explored fractal trees. In that unit, we were tasked to create a program that created a GUI window that allowed users to create their own fractal trees. 

In order to create this window, we used a graphics class that was implemented for us by our teacher. We were then told to manipulate this class to create our own program. I spilt up the creation of the fractal trees by making different sliders for the parts of the tree: the amount of levels for the tree, the angle (theta) that the branches had, and the scale factor. I then had buttons for different methods the user would need, like an exit, clear, and draw button. I also created a button that made another window pop up, which explained the program and its purpose. Lastly, for some fun, I had 4 different buttons that created a different fractal tree for each season. When the user would press one of those buttons, a tree with specific colors and shapes depending on the season would pop up, as well as a photo background correlating with the season. 

What was challenging for me was how to incorporate all these different elements in my main function. I had so many moving parts of the program, so figuring out how I could bring them all together was tough. In order to solve this, I made sure to map out all my thoughts on paper. Writing down and drawing diagrams of how everything related to each other, and how I need to outline my code, helped me figure out how to code the most important part of my program. I honestly had so much fun coding this project, as well as all the other projects in this class, and I would be so excited to do the same through this club!

My freshman summer I worked as a full-stack developer intern at Ellucian, an education technology company. Over the summer, I helped design Ellucian’s regulatory framework proof of concept (POC). The primary goal of the POC was to build a dynamic form builder similar to google forms. This form would then be used in student data collection. The purpose behind the POC was the following; there are regulatory bodies such as HESA in the UK (Higher Education Statistics Agency) or governments as a whole that require specific information to be collected from universities; however, these regulatory bodies constantly change their requirements, so there exists a need for a form that can collect data and also change dynamically.
The Regulatory framework POC had one main part: building a Template Builder interface that allowed an admin to design a form with questions, question types (dropdown, multiple choice, short answer, etc.), as well as a data source or API that that question would be connected to. As the form was being built, I implemented the code to build a metadata JSON template in the background filled with the information the admin was selecting. This JSON template could then be uploaded to a renderer page in which the template would be dynamically rendered, and the answer to each question would be pre-populated with data from the APIs the admin selected per question. The idea was that as the JSON template changed, the renderer page would automatically render a new form. I ran into all sorts of bugs along the way, especially bugs relating to asynchronous vs. synchronous calls. It’s a bit complicated to explain the project in its entirety, but I predominantly used React.js and the MUI library on the front end and then used Express.js on the backend. I was proud of the project because it forced me to tackle my imposter syndrome, and there were so many learnings I gained in the process.

This past summer, I interned at a healthcare-tech company called AS Software. I worked on a three-person intern team to build AS-CloudFax, a project that allows healthcare professionals to fax medical reports and images while eliminating the need for on-premises faxing hardware and server infrastructure. AS-CloudFax is cloud-native, multi-tenant, and designed to encrypt and transmit sensitive data securely.

We built AS-CloudFax with the Rust programming language, a web framework called Actix-Web, and a PostgreSQL database. AS-CloudFax exposes a REST API that incorporates webhooks to deliver real-time updates about sent faxes. Requests are authenticated and validated for format and idempotency.

The project took us 11 weeks to build, but unfortunately we (the interns) were not able to see the project get integrated into the company's existing .NET web app. Still, we were able to build the entire back-end during our internship which was really special.

All 3 of us were brand new to Rust and Postgres, and the only other back-end development experience I'd had prior was from CS20 which was a soft intro at best. We were given guidance from our higher-ups, but we were mostly left alone to figure out our problems and learn the languages/technologies on our own.

We spent many hours googling, sifting through Stack Overflow and the Rust docs, and looking through legacy company code to figure things out. We constantly ran into new problems as we got used to the many different technologies we had to use. For example, we would have a segment of code that was passing every unit test and integration test, but would fail when deployed to Kubernetes. This forced us to learn how the different components of our project interacted with each other so that we could isolate the problem and find a solution.

We learned to work, communicate, and delegate tasks very effectively with each other, and we became exponentially more productive as we learned how to use the resources we had. We also learned how to formulate good questions to ask when we were stuck. We grew from struggling through a basic Rust "hello world" exercise to being able to stand up an endpoint, unit test and integration test it, and have it ready for a Github pull request in a single morning.

My first professional web engineering experience was challenging, but I came away a better programmer, and I built software that will be used by thousands of clients every day.

One of the biggest problems that The Lantern is tackling is that the way of thinking in the technical world is not varied enough in the current day and age. This is something I strongly resonate with because I have noticed firsthand a persisting lack of diversity in the tech world. While there have been many efforts to promote diversity in the STEM world, there is still a large disparity in many corporate environments, which can lead to a lack of perspective and new thinking. Outside of diversity, Computer Science is a discipline that must have some degree of intersectionality. With that said, ALL of those voices from other disciplines must be included in the conversation to create a successful product / solution, not just the technical voices. 

I also agree with their second problem of the general public lacking access to academic and expert information in tech. Even as a CS student, I find myself struggling to keep up to date with the latest trends in the industry. There doesn't seem to be many resources to better educate people about the current events in the tech world. All the cities I visited, Beijing, Qingdao, and Tianjin had street cleaners that would regularly sweep and pickup litter from the sidewalks. The summer after my freshman year, I was interested in getting involved with the Textbook Exchange Network on campus, specifically with contributing to their data analytics effort. One of their goals was to create a KPI analytics dashboard to provide stakeholders, including Board Members and school representatives, with insights on the health and wellness of the Textbook Exchange Network program, both as a whole and at each member university. Storytelling with data has always been a skill I’ve sought to improve, and I jumped at the opportunity to create a data report. After researching different platforms to easily build data apps, I decided to teach myself how to use Streamlit, an open-source app framework in Python.

Creating a data app from scratch was challenging in several ways. It forced me to improve my Python skills, which were rudimentary at best, and definitely tested my patience. However, I found that it was a fun exercise to think of different metrics I could create from the available data on our buyer and seller databases. This included the number of textbook buyers and sellers, the breakdown of transaction type (cash or credit), the distribution of textbook listing and selling prices, the breakdown of textbook sales per department (e.g. French, economics, etc), and more. After brainstorming what metrics to collect, I leveraged SQL queries on our databases to extract these insights. From there, I experimented with different ways of presenting this data, and sought to make my charts as interactive as possible. This included hover functionality and different filters. Finally, I presented the finished product to the board of the Textbook Exchange Network nonprofit, explaining trends in customer behavior and book sales within the student textbook marketplace and providing recommendations to increase textbook sales. Witnessing the impact of my insights on organizational decision-making and strategy was empowering. I thoroughly enjoyed the process of extracting insights from unorganized data and finding the most effective way to present them.

Couple years ago I started a class project, which was completely up to us to find a client and decide what to do with it. It was a great way to experience how to build something from scratch on my own. My friend was working on his own start up, so after few conversations we agreed that a Management System for Inventory, Clients and Invoicing would be a cool project to help his company.  

The project was a Desktop Application, that had three main functions. The main section was Invoicing, as it would not only create a pdf file with all the information from the purchase, but also update the database of clients and inventory. The management for clients consisted on a database that stores contact information and a register of all purchases made by the client. The management for inventory stored all the available products with a unique ID, quantity in stock and a threshold number for an alarm to the user once the quantity goes below that number. All databases had to be updatable at all times by the user. 

Technology wise, the backend and GUI was developed using Java. The database was designed in MySQL workbench and hosted in MySQL.

The project came with many challenges because most of these technologies were new for me. Even though I was familiar with Java syntax and concepts like OOP, it was my first time coding a project by myself. I spent many hours learning about Java Swing GUI elements and flow control to connect all screens in a User friendly way. I also did a crash course in SQL to learn about queries. Another challenge was figuring out how to connect the database with the program itself, and then how to create an executable that could be shared with my client. However, I feel I underestimated the time and importance of design stage, establishing a Criteria for Success, and meeting with my client to make sure everything was going well. It was useful to practice abstraction and design before rushing into code and therefore saving time. 

I recognize the code could be organized more efficiently, and adding more in-line comments would also make the code more readable. In general, the program could use some restructuring, so I am in the stage of designing those changes. 

It was a useful experience to assess my skills and understand the value of documentation and planning before coding.

column15:
Coding tickles.

For our final project in Intro to Programming, I knew I had to make something absolutely bonkers: it was a chance to render my destiny fulfilled, to create what had kept me company from childhood, to code a videogame. 

Space Invaders.

It was an ambitious undertaking, considering I had so little knowledge of anything programming (at the time). I had begun by building the foundation -- a space background, a spaceship that shot lasers, and alien targets. Even this proved a challenge. I couldn't get the "aliens" to disappear after being shot, neither could I get them to move. It seemed I had bitten more than I could chew; so I broke my project into smaller parts, and approached it scientifically. While bug testing, I'd change one variable -- see the outcome, note its results -- and accordingly, figure out how to solve any coding problem. If I couldn't figure it out this way, I'd consult GitHub or YouTube. 

After some time, I got into the rhythm of things, and fixed my issues. I had built momentum --and oh boy, was I addicted to the momentum. Over the coming weeks, a mantra rung, rung, and rung: how could I make this the most unnecessarily intricate project ever? 

Every night after dinner, I’d devote long hours that always felt too short, to adding or bug-fixing a new feature. I’d create different modes of varying difficulties, or even throw in a Pac-Man final boss battle, for example. As I continued to convolute my game, bugs buzzed out of every corner, to a point where even my teacher couldn’t zap them away. 

Regardless, programming problems were never an issue: tinkering away at Eclipse made all sense of exhaust disappear, largely due to the “coding tickle” phenomena. 
That tickle after rectifying a painstakingly gruesome bug — when you get that rush of profound self-satisfaction, where you sit back, and think hey, I just did that — leaves you with nothing but an explosive smile. 

I reflect that's why I kept adding complications: more problems meant more solutions, and in turn, more tickle. 

Ultimately, programming has taught me to seek challenge, to hope for the unknown, for only then, will my success successfully feel successful. For this reason , I hope to join JumboCode. I hope to find more problems, and ultimately, I hope to fix them.

The project that I feel particularly proud of is Gerp, which is the project that culminates at the end of Data Structures. Gerp is meant to function as a searching tool, finding any given word within any given directory, and is supposed to be able to run within certain time and space constraints. Gerp was built in C++ and runs on the terminal. In addition, Gerp is a pair programming project.
	One of the main challenges I faced when working with Gerp was pair programming. It is one thing to sit in your room and type away at your keyboard, and another thing to code while explaining what you wrote to your partner. I often found myself stuck because I couldn’t quite articulate what I wanted to accomplish, or I had to wrap my head around my partner’s idea (which, in most cases, was different from my own). Communicating while programming taught me to become much more deliberate with my code, and it showed me how to understand someone else’s thought process. 
	The second challenge I faced was designing. Never before did I have to worry about time and space complexity, and then my partner and I had to come up with a design that was as efficient as possible. For the first time, I had to sit down and draw out my entire idea before getting to coding. At first, I found planning difficult, because it felt very abstract as compared to coding. However, working with a partner allowed both of us to talk out our various design ideas and come up with a decent solution to Gerp, giving us a roadmap and saving us countless hours in the coding process.

column15:
A project I'm proud of is the SeaPerchII project I worked on last year. My work on SeaPerchII consisted mainly of building and designing two of the modules: IR sensors and whiskers. My work on the IR sensor consisted of designing a silicone mold that could waterproof a land IR-sensor, and then programming the code to report data back to an Arduino microprocessor. I built the mold for the IR sensor by using Solidworks to design and 3D print a case for the sensor. I then casted silicone into this 3D case, which protected the sensor's electronics, but I ran into a challenge with the programming/data. Because the IR was underwater, the readings for distance were skewed (light absorbed differently in water). I solved this challenge by taking physical readings of output voltage vs measured distance, and then programming an algorithm that would change the distance data based on this new equation. The algorithm would also filter outlier data via a moving average.

The other module I worked on was whiskers, which consist of a conductive grease path (acting as a resistor) embedded in a silicone mold. When stretched, it changes resistance, which can be sensed. I built the mold for the whiskers by CADing a 3D case that would set the shape for the silicone to be casted in. Then, I pathed conductive grease and wires through the whisker and added a q-tip in the middle, functionally turning the whisker into a variable resistor that would change resistance when touched. From there, I programmed an algorithm in Arduino that could sense these changes in resistance based on current and recent voltage averages. It could then trigger an output, such as redirecting motors, based on a distortion/resistance change. For this module, the biggest challenge was simply the fabrication:  I went through six different 3D molds and three different methods of sensing resistance changes. I ended up settling on a three-step casting mold and a voltage divider for data reading, which I found to be the most consistent.  And after constructing hundreds of different whiskers and taking countless underwater data/code trials, I finally discovered the ideal version.

column15: This summer, I came across a cool project that utilized an API that interacted with open-source AI models to restore user's uploaded images. I found the API to be interesting as it made AI generation so simple. I found out about all the different AI models that was open-sourced and decided to see if I could create a website that generated Instagram captions using an AI model called Salesforce Blip which transcribed uploaded images into descriptions of them. I found that the API I discovered lacked capabilities and speed (and also behind a paywall RIP) so I found a new API called Hugging Face. I combined a free Photo Uploader API called Uploader (I think they rebranded to ByteUploader now) with that API and OpenAI API to generate "creative" captions for the uploaded images. After a bunch of trail-and-error with the structure of the API calls and handling the different stages of user interaction to get from start to finish in a NextJS, Tailwind, and Typescript frontend, I faced a big problem with hosting and how hosting on Vercel gave users an infinite loop of generating but no result. I diagnosed the problem to a timed out API request in the Google Chrome console and traced it back to Vercel's free hosting limiting API calls to only 10 seconds. This led me to learn a new hosting, Netlify, which was able to handle the API calls. Now the website is up at https://captionator.netlify.app/. During the project, I faced another big problem which was rate limiting user's ability to generate and regenerate captions since OpenAI is behind a paywall. To solve this, I had to research and incorporate another database called Upstash Redis, where a big problem was that it counted failed generations as used generations. Thus, I had to work on a front-end redirection system as well as integrating it with NextAuth Google Authentication in order to be prevent users from generating past their rate limiter.

I worked on a personal project at the end of my last year of high school to join my interests in research and environmental science. My goal was to evaluate the average understanding of climate change among students at my school, so I designed a survey that asked the students to quantify the magnitude of several changes that climate change is predicted to incite (sea level rise, average temperature rise, and biodiversity loss to name a few). 

Designing the survey was challenging because I had to sift through lots of dense information and choose what I wanted to highlight in my questions, but I found it to be manageable because that was under my control. My biggest setbacks were logistical—it was very difficult to get my student body to actually respond to my survey! I had to enlist the help of lots of my teachers and send many emails, but eventually I got my principal to send the survey to all students, and from there I asked lots of teachers to ask their students to complete my survey.

Once I passed those challenges, I used predicted metrics from the IPCC’s 2022 report as my baseline and I tested for statistically significant results once several hundred students responded to my survey. I then got to share my findings that depicted where most students overestimated or underestimated a given effect of climate change, and discovered that making a project out of my own interest could lead to valid and informative claims.

https://pmelga01.itch.io/pixelart-character-customizer

 I was asked to design the CS11 Teaching Assistant merchandise, a symbol of our team's hard work and dedication to our love of teaching. While this task was daunting, I had a vision of **everybody** being able to contribute to the design of the merch in some shape or form, that is what was most important to me at the end of the day. 

I took the opportunity to re-design and improve a character customizer code I had written for a summer internship that originally took me weeks to complete, I aimed to take the parts I learned in those weeks to adapt it in two weeks for the design of the merchandise. I used Unity's Game Engine to build the scenes I needed from scratch. I put together all the UI, buttons, and event scripts in order to make it interactive and easy to navigate. 

One of my biggest issues I faced was figuring out whether a WebGL Unity build had image exporting capabilities, as it was something I had never done before but wanted to add in order to standardize all characters created to the proper size and resolution I wanted. I spent days researching, watching YouTube videos, following forum threads, some saying it couldn't be done, until I finally found a Unity plug-in I could copy and adapt into my code in order to get the functionality I wanted. I merged the plug-in idea with another local exporter that was working in order to get the high-quality images and file types to take into photoshop. 

The second challenge I faced, which was a design challenge/choice I made for myself was to have the character choices and settings persist across different scenes. each asset menu is a unique Unity Scene. I had to plan for ways I could re-use scripts and code for different pieces of the character asset selector, as well as introducing the back-tracking option for better user experience so one wouldn't have to reset all their hard-work. This meant ensuring the buttons consistently would load the chosen settings for each menu as well.

The character design, asset variation, animations, and simple UI design was implemented for fun as a break from any code bugs I faced along the way. I loved this project because it was a silly start of an idea turned into a final product that made a ton of people smile.

column15: In my AP computer science class, I completed a project called ‘RideShare’. RideShare took a straight 31-mile road with stations located at each mile and simulated ride-share app. One of the many cars would start off at a random station, a destination, and a capacity to pick up three people maximum. Each of the 31 stations had a random amount of passengers all with a destination. If a car came along and was traveling in the right direction, it would pick up passengers if possible and attempt to deliver them to their destination. Drivers got paid per passenger per mile and we had to keep track of the revenue. There were a lot of other specific rules and regulations I had to adhere to in this simulation. In this project, it was ridiculously difficult to keep track of all the moving parts. I made four different classes: Car class, Passenger class, and Station class. I placed all the passengers in an array and kept track of their destinations. To keep track of my program, I printed out the car as a string to keep track of all passengers and destinations. I created many functions in the sub-classes in order to make the Car class more organized and manageable to program and print out. Finally, I printed out the revenue from each ride and the miles driven by the car. Changing every variable during every single mile was very difficult to maintain but by using many many many if-else statements I managed to build an efficient ride-share simulation.

But, I was able to give some joy with the elderly and youth population (I'll talk about in the next prompt).

Taking my first two introduction classes made me realize the disparities I faced could be solved through online applications/technologies. Information, such as rallies to the city hall for housing rights, food bank refills, and discounted groceries, is far more efficient and accessible for whole communities through the Internet. The capabilities of software is quite endless, but I want to create things that align with my values, and I truly value JumboCode's mission.

I have been a part of a non-profit organization called Chinatown Community Development Center, for the past 5 years. I joined CCDC because it gave me the resources (funding and space) to host events with the elderly population. They loved making red envelope crafts because it reminded them of their youth. This past summer, I designed an intro to CS course for low-income high school kids. This idea sparked from my horrible experiences of AP CS classes in high school. They were weak 
that only covered basic functions of Scratch (an elementary block coding program). More so, there is not a CS curriculum within the district so all the other schools were struggling as well. I wanted to relay my view on CS and spark any interest in my students.
In my curriculum, I enforced the idea of team discussion environments (such as labs), live coding demos, and the workflow of exploring ideas online. I utilized assignments from my CS11 class and the intro class of UCBerkeley to create a rigorous yet effective course. This course focused on foundational concepts of Boolean logic, functions, and OOP. This course reached 6 students due to limited resources. 

One more project I like to highlight is my work in the non-profit called Beyond Differences this past March. Our mission is to tackle the issues of social isolation within our school system. Issues related to cultural differences, learning abilities, racial/gender aspects, and more. I facilitated 20 high school youth to develop a curriculum to dissolve social isolation related to immigrant and Asian issues. Our curriculum reached 5000 schools nationwide with many integrating to their system. This was an important project to me because we were able to integrate it into many schools in SF. It helped with the transition of immigrants into the system, through specialized classes with a focus on sharing of cultural aspects and acceptance of others.

This past summer, I self taught web development alongside taking CS15. The project I am most proud of is a Task Manager website. It was my first project after learning the basics of the MERN stack through videos. I utilized Nodejs and MongoDB to handle requests and responses for the objects/models of my tasks. This was connected with RESTapi for client side posts/gets/deleles. React/CSS handled the front end to create an aesthetic and simple layout for adding/deleting/completing tasks. 

Since this was my first project, I constantly had to visit resources to understand how to connect DB, APIs, requests/responses, and the front end. One of my first challenges was to simply start up the local server and connect it to my mongoDB host. This took time to understand the libraries and frameworks needed (express, cors, mongoose). My next challenge was to create a task object to contain information. It was challenging but comfortable to adapt to the javascript environments. The biggest issue I came across was that the server was not properly listing all the tasks. My get calls only printed out the first task that was added into the database. The good thing was that I had a workflow implemented. I isolated my problem with the express calling because my posts through REST were going through. So I first looked at more videos on arrow functions to access the express framework but didn't solve it. I looked on Stackoverflow and did not find my solution. Then, I asked a friend with back end experience and he saw that my function should have been asynchronous. That solved it, just one "async". 

The best lesson I got out of my first project is the workflow aspect when I need help. I know to look for resources either through videos or Stackoverflow with more specific questions. If that doesn't work, I don't shy away from asking my peers so I can learn faster and fix the problem. I enjoy collaborating with people which makes me adapt well to new learning environments.
