column15: One project I worked on that I’m proud of was creating a process flow chart for my internship in 2022 where I worked as an Information Security Intern. There, I was tasked with creating a flow chart (playbook) and a corresponding information document for our Service Desk and Security team to follow that would help them handle incoming email incidents and security threats. It was a pretty daunting task to create a flow chart for such a large range of cybersecurity incidents but it was fun to break down and tackle. I started by writing down the different types of incidents and how to detect, investigate, and remediate each one. I then handled daily email incidents myself and recorded the type of incident I received as well as the threat level and other relevant information. After a couple days, I had both a list of different incidents as well as ways to solve them and (combining with my brainstorming notes) was able to create a good list containing all the different types of cases. Some challenges I ran into was having too many cases to create a concise flow chart as it initially had too many branches. I solved this by creating what I found to be the 6 biggest subgroups, Malicious Links, Spam, Spoofing, Attachments, Phone Calls, and Impersonations. I then developed the flow chart for each of those subcases (which contained decision, process, and subprocess nodes). Another difficulty in keeping the flow chart concise was with the density of information rather than the amount of nodes. To solve this, I decided to purposely keep the flow chart to a general overview to help people understand the workflow and created a separate corresponding information document which contained detailed documentation on how to handle each of the nodes. I am very proud of this playbook as both the Service Desk and Security team expressed gratitude for creating this to linearize a previously unorganized workflow and to reduce the loads of both teams. I returned to intern at this company again this past summer and it was really rewarding to talk to my manager and see that they were still using the playbook I created.

In the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, being bored and running out of things to do, I decided to combine several passions of mine–video editing, animated TV shows, music, and the art of meme-making–into a glorious creation: a full kazoo-cover and music video recreation of the theme song of one of my favorite shows, The Owl House. I knew that such a feat would not be easy, but yet I proceeded to get this project into action. First I would have to create the audio: a full orchestral arrangement of the original theme song composed of many tracks of me playing the kazoo. I thought this should be easy enough, so I jumped right into it, picking out various parts of the original song by ear and recreating them on individual voice memo files on my phone. However, I soon realized how inefficient and difficult this was. Even though I had labeled each of the files accordingly before sending them over to my computer, it was hard and time-consuming to put them together one-by-one. It was also difficult to figure out how to fill in empty spaces in the music, as I was improvising some of the parts as I went, which wasn’t going as smoothly as I’d hoped. Had I planned my process out better, I would have thought about recording directly onto my computer, or creating a slightly more cohesive arrangement of the song (even though it was supposed to be a meme, I wanted it to sound as much like the real thing as I could given that it was played on kazoos).
I took this into consideration as I moved onto the second part: the visuals. For this, I took the time to divide up the various animated scenes of the theme song video, and tried to come up with how I would recreate each scene and replace all of the characters with kazoos. Not having the supplies or crew of an actual filmmaker, I knew I was going to have to be creative with how I went about the rest of this one-person feat. Over the next few weeks, I used photo-editors to recreate backgrounds using a mouse, color picker, and a digital paintbrush tool, filmed kazoos moving in the same ways that the characters did in front of a makeshift green screen made out of green masking tape, and taught myself how to use keyframes in Final Cut to make images move across the video screen.
After many hours of work, I had finally finished my masterpiece. Although it wasn’t necessarily perfect, which it of course didn’t have to be given my circumstances and the humorous intent of the project, I was amazed to see how I made a silly idea I randomly had one day turn into something real that I could see right before my own eyes. All the time and effort I had put into it had been worth it, as I was able to create something that I was proud of and had a really fun time making, even if the audience for it might be kind of niche. But I still decided to post my creation on YouTube, and see what would become of it. As of today, the video has 33K views online, which isn’t too bad in my opinion, and I can only hope that it has brought some joy into someone’s day. Having that ability to connect with and have an impact on someone I may never actually see face to face, through something I worked hard to create was such a cool feeling, and one that I hope can be brought about by more of the projects I work on in the future ;)

Using Swift and the Xcode IDE, I built an iOS application centered around the concept of augmented reality (AR) medical cards. Through the camera feed, the application would scan these uniquely created ID cards and animate 3D overlays of health information into view with real-time tracking. The data would also simultaneously be imported into a separate tab on the application that maintained the provider’s current patient roster and all pertinent information for convenient viewing. For the most part, it was intended to pair the patient verification process with enhanced data visualization, and I experimented with ARKit in order to implement a medium for this that starkly contrasted what you might expect.

Almost unsurprisingly, the majority of the bugs I encountered came about through the AR environment I was attempting to construct. Often, the lighting was off, the scaling didn’t make sense, the animations weren’t running smoothly, or the program stopped recognizing the cards altogether. Dealing with the overall look of the application and its interactive elements was a slow and (occasionally) tedious process. It required immense attention to detail and a great deal of patience as I generated and regenerated entire libraries of content. Still, this was one of my favorite projects because it allowed me to have free reign over this simple scanner idea that blossomed into a more complex application. I enjoyed the challenge of creating my own virtual world populated with medical data, and I look forward to extending it even further with facial recognition and possibly peripheral device connections.

I had a group 'design make test' project to improve a winter Olympic sport and after brainstorming 96 ideas we settled on improving Paralympic curling - in regular curling you have someone throw a stone and two others to move with it and sweep. The Paralympic version completely lacks the latter part, which we felt was more than half the event. The biggest challenges were making a wheelchair that could safely be controlled on ice (especially when the athletes were sweeping), and designing a way to quickly let the broom be accessed and stowed, as well as ensuring they were positioned in a way that would let them put down enough force easily. We broke down the tasks and wanted to ensure we consulted people with experience in the sport to ensure we met their needs.
We were fortunate enough to get an initial consultation with the coach of the team UK Paralympic curling team (and former Paralympian) at the start of the project before they competed in the 2014 Sochi Olympic games, and then were able to get in touch with a curling club in Scotland to get measurements for forces needed and other considerations, as well as convinced an ice skating rink (the only one that would agree) to let us test friction and control of different materials.
Once we finished making it we returned to the rink to test it out and had a catch up with the coach again and were really happy to hear their response to our developments and felt that we had properly addressed their needs as an athlete.

column15: The most exciting project I worked on was in 40, which was Arith. My partner and I had to build an image compressor/decompressor and it involved a lot of steps and floating point arithmetic. The implementation process of the compressor/decompressor was broken down in to 7 steps each, with step 1 of the compressor corresponding to step 7 of the decompressor, step 2 corresponding with step 6, etc. The idea was we had to work backwards on the decompressor so we could test the functionality of both programs before inching forward. The steps involved modifying data representation, floating point arithmetic, bit manipulation, and lots of careful testing with different images. What was difficult for my partner and I was fully understanding why each step was taking place and how that step would lead us closer to the finish line. We spent a lot of time drawing out examples and asking TAs questions. This project is one of my favorites because it was nothing like my previous projects and it involved a lot of small, intricate tasks. It was cool to see how each step brought us closer to our goal and the satisfaction when both programs worked hand-in-hand was significant. My partner and I also became good friends as we bonded over hours of debugging together.

My senior year of high school, for my CS class, we had to do a final project of our choosing, but it had to be a *real* project, with an actual client, an activity log, the works. And so I decided I should do something for my mom. My mom owned a restaurant at the time, and had been complaining about how the format in which Square provided bulk exported order data was awful because it forced her to manually reorganize the data (apparently there was no tool in Sheets/Excel to remedy this), row by row, in a spreadsheet to get it into a form that was usable. And so, naturally, I decided that THIS would be my project. It was much, much bigger than I anticipated it would be.
For one, this ballooned into such a momentous task because just nothing I wanted to do came free. Everything had some issue, everything had to be learned from scratch. For example, for my macro plan I wanted a script that ran in Google Drive. Sure. Only-- that's in GAS, which is in JavaScript, which I had never used before at the time. So I had to learn JS, then the GAS basics, and then the various GAS API idiosyncrasies (who knew a "Sheet" was an entirely different object to a "Spreadsheet"). And all this was made more complicated by the fact that I had actually never worked with a spreadsheet before either, and even more so because no one around me could help with anything technical past the JS step. I have a screenshot somewhere of my browser with so many different GAS docs and W3 page tabs open that each one is only a little nub showing the icon and the first letter of the page title.
Second, I realized I actually couldn't just get to coding like in class, I actually needed an implementation plan, a platform, and I needed to sit down and interview my mom and note down specs on what the program should have as IO and what kind of UI she wanted, etc. And we'd have to reconvene and I'd have to debrief her every time I hit some critical roadblock, and pitch to her various small changes that could make the project possible, and/or possible for me finish in time.
The third and final thing was that this was by far the largest project by code volume I'd ever written. With absolutely no training in writing actual production code as a highschooler with one CS class under their belt, I will never live down the fact that I had the foresight to very carefully structure my program and give it some form of modularity. Even if that was lots and lots of helper functions. I even had a testing secondary "main" function which would run these functions individually using handmade data or example spreadsheets I got from my mom. I had no style guide, and going back I see all the comments I left.
To me, the craziest part is that it worked, and worked smoothly. I don't think I even fully appreciated what it was that I'd accomplished when I finished it; I was too busy with other schoolwork. And in spite of the fact that the whole thing became obsolete when the restaurant closed down soon after, I've never been more proud of a project than this one, to date.

I am extremely proud of my gerp project from CS15 last semester. I pair programmed with my partner Ella who has been a very special person throughout my entire CS journey at Tufts. We worked hours and hours each day to perfect that project, and it felt like a culmination of my year of learning computer science at Tufts. It was not an easy project at all, but it really taught me about my own capabilities and collaborating effectively with a partner. The main reason that I look back on that project with so much pride is because if I had told the version of myself from even a year ago that I would have accomplished something like that, I would have been truly astonished.
We built the project after a long period of designing our hash table structure. We spent days toiling over our design to accout for space and time constraints all while learning about a data structure that was completely new to us. We thought our design was great, and we were eager to start coding. After a few days, we coded, took care of some small bugs, and we thought we were done! (what a funny thought). After our first version, we tested smallGutenberg, and it literally took 30 minutes to run. We spent a day in the trenches figuring that out. Then, medium worked and we thought we were in the clear! We still had a week left, and we were shocked with our progress. Then, we heard the largeGutenberg test file was being run. We ran the test, crossed our fingers, and hoped for the best. The best was, unfortunately, not met. We had to go back to the drawing board so we could run the test under memory and time constraints. We modified our structure, decided to store our data in a vector of vectors to account for space, and we crossed our fingers again after another visit to the trenches. It ran! But... we had diff output. Back to the drawing board we went. We figured out we had to sift through our code to add a couple more conditons, THEN we were in the clear. Everything worked perfectly!
We truly persevered throughout this project. We were overconfident, had our confidence shot down by some massively tragic bugs, but we still made it through. We spent some nights coding on the JCC 4th floor until 1am. Our weekends were swallowed by this project. But, at the end of the day, we did not give up and now it is something I look back on with fond memories and immense pride over my teamwork with Ella and everything that came with this project. It felt like my true initiation into the world of CS and completely changed my perspective regarding my own CS abilities, and it leaves me wanting to take on more and more challenging projects.

column15:
This past summer, my intern team at Mitre built a fullstack application from scratch that
had an interactive map UI that a user could select a region on and get US Air force data on that region. This could be anything from weather information to region specific information to target locations. It was a daunting task to be presented with at the beginning of the summer for sure. I didn't know where to start. None of the technologies that they were using was I familiar enough with to just jump into coding, so for about a week or two, I researched and learned C#, how to build .Net console applications, what an S3 bucket was, the differences between typescript and javascript and what a react redux thunk is. We also had to think about how to build the application. What sorts of things should our application do? What are its limitations? What design choices will make for fast and easy communication between microservices? After this learning period was over, the team started building this application from the backend, first handling the ability for the user to upload files to a resource server that would then go on to handle indexing them into a mongoDB. I started slow admittedly, as I was becoming familiar with C#, but after a while, the team started to really make meaningful strides toward our goal. We integrated a MongoDB database with our console application and everything was working. Users could upload files and they would appear in our database. But as soon as I was beginning to become really comfortable with C# .NET, we had to start to work on the UI, which meant another week of learning and researching. But at the end of the summer, I looked back on the work that we did as a team and I was so impressed and proud of what we were able to accomplish. It seemed impossible at the beginning of the summer, but taking time to learn the technologies in conjunction with an incredibly supportive team allowed us to accomplish our goal and come away with a meaningful project that I can say I was proud to work on.

column15:
One project that really excited me was my final project in the Honors Computer Science class I took in 11th grade, which was a collaborative project among our class of about 12 students. The objective of the project was to create a flight booking application, where a user could build their flight itinerary by entering information about their itinerary and book their flight based on the flight options generated by the program. 

This project required implementing the frontend and backend of the application, with the front end executing the user interface element of the product. As a part of the backend, our objective was to be able to filter and sort through a large Excel dataset of flights in order to find all options for the given itinerary. In addition, we wanted to sort these flight options in order from fastest to slowest total travel time to offer users the most optimal itineraries. When designing the program, we chose to use a Python library called OpenPyXL, which allowed us to create a pipeline from the Excel spreadsheet to our Python program. Within the backend, I was responsible with indexing out of the Excel dataset in order to display the correct flight results based on the user’s search.

Due to the large-scale nature of this project, a challenge that we faced as a group was assembling and testing our program. Each student was responsible for a component of the program’s implementation. Having an updated and functional version of each component in order to test the main file throughout the project was extremely difficult because students  developed each component at varying paces and often ran into issues in their program which delayed our collective schedule. Although we tested each component individually throughout the project, ensuring that they worked cohesively for the final product was difficult when each component was not complete at the same time. 

Despite these challenges, I thoroughly enjoyed working in a collaborative, team-oriented environment on a computer science project after primarily having written and designed programs individually until then. Being able to work with other students in order to understand their varying perspectives and approaches to logic and problem-solving made the project extremely engaging and impactful in my growth as a programmer and developer. In addition, being able to work amongst a product team to create a high-level, innovative product was instrumental in elevating my passion for computer science and broadening my understanding and interest in professional software development.

column15: While it may be a response you get quite often I really enjoyed working on arith in 40. My partner and I were challenged with designing, building, and testing an image compressor and decompressor built in C. The compression strategy took place over multiple steps of translation and conversion, including quantization, reclassification, and bit-packing, utilizing principles behind JPEG image compression and broadcast color TV. Starting with our nearly twenty-page specification, we worked to ingest and synthesize the information into a design document that would specify our program flow and testing. This design explored expected parameters, outputs, processes, and edge cases for each step of the compression and decompression process, provided both would be implemented in parallel in order to test each step separately. This stepwise progression of implementation held true to another fundamental aspect of the project; modularity. While there was one greater goal for the program, we understood the most readable and test-friendly code would be broken up into several chunks. Some of the said chunks would be as simple as casting integers to floats, and others would be a bit more intricate, utilizing the discrete cosine transformation to quantize pixel values. We also implemented a self-standing bit-packing interface that would be used during the final compression stage. This was created to be a universal tool for anyone wanting to represent information in a 64-bit word, allowing for least significant bit and width-based location retrieval and editing. While completing our design, we estimated the necessary time for each step and planned out our schedules for the two weeks given for the project. Learning about the history of image compression, whether it be simple conversions people do on their own laptops, or how analog engineers made black and white TVs backward-compatible with color by converting between RGB and component, was quite a fascinating journey.

SpeakOUT
In high school, I was completely closeted. There weren’t many other gay people in my school, and bullies said terrible things about the kids who were out. At that time, coming out felt like an impossibility. A thing that one thinks about in the abstract, but that one knows is never going to actually happen. Winning the lottery. Traveling to the moon. Coming out as gay.

Though I went to a religious school, we were fortunate enough to have to take a class on gender and sexuality in senior year. Most of the curriculum was out of date and kind of hokey, except one key aspect: every other week or so, the teachers got a guest speaker to come and speak to us, a queer alum of my high school. And these weren’t adults that I couldn’t relate to! I had known these people in high school. I had known some of them while they were in the closet themselves. They talked about their lives after high school. About how in high school, it really was hard, for all of the idiosyncratic reasons that it was hard for me to come out in my community, but that it got better. I don’t know if I really understood that it got better until I got to college, but their words, however insignificant they may have seemed, gave me the hope to keep on believing in a future where I could be fully myself. I want to help connect SpeakOUT volunteers with LGBTQ folk because I know that being in an affinity space where people understand the implicit experiences you have had as a result of your identity is invaluable.

Theater@First

I love theater! I’ve been fortunate enough to have grown up and seen broadway shows, regional theater, and everything in between. But what I really love about theater is how it can make us feel about ourselves. In high school, I was cast as the lead in a play. I was terrified at the mountain of lines I had to memorize. I was in every scene (this is NOT a flex - I was the only one who volunteered for the part). Slowly but surely, I learned my lines, and standing up on stage, confident as all hell, and knowing every word of my monologue felt so. Damn. Good.

I want to help Theater@First with their props because I know that for both the actors, crew and audience alike, theater has the power to change lives.

column15: Last fall, I took a class at Tufts called programming for math. For the last project, we coded a neural network in python, mostly from scratch. It was able to take in photos of hand written digits, and guess what the number is. The professor wrote some starter code (like the backward pass) and gave it to us to figure out. Even though at times I was more confused than I have ever been, the moment the digits started showing up I realized it was all worth it. We first talked about the general structure of the network, what activation function we would be using, and a little linear algebra background. Then we started working on the forward pass, which helped solidify a lot of the things we talked about. For the training process, we took batches of weight and updated them and calculated loss and accuracy to watch the network grow. And lastly we graphed all of our data to find an optimal batch size. The most challenging part of this process was figuring it all out alone, especially since it was my first semester coding. I felt very overwhelmed and confused, but managed to figure it out by being chronically on YouTube. This turned out to be the most exciting coding project I have worked on at Tufts and ever since, I have been hoping to expand it so that instead of just digits, it can read hand written pages and make it into a pdf.

One project that I am proud of is my Theology Project titled “Shinto and Christian Divinity and Spirituality in Everyday Life: An Analysis of Miyazaki’s Spirited Away and Pixar’s Soul.” The Theology Project is a year-long project in which students are tasked with researching a religious topic (I went to a Catholic high school), producing a final paper, and conducting an hour-long presentation in front of the class/school community. 

My research process began in September 2020 with looking at academic journals, books, and articles trying to get any sense of my topic. This first phase of my research was quite difficult as I realized I was not super interested in researching religious histories or figures and wanted something more interdisciplinary. Through exploring more articles, I slowly constructed my broad framework of the intersection between film and religion. Reflecting on my own experiences and interests, however, is how I found my focus on comparing the films Spirited Away and Soul and their respective Christian and Shinto messages. I enjoyed watching these films with my family and have connections to these two religions, which made my research process much more enjoyable and interesting.

Another major challenge I faced was managing my time. With a project this big, I realized that I had to accumulate progress throughout the year. Every week I tried to work on something–whether that was adding to my research, creating slides, or writing my paper–and slowly but surely made progress. The last few days before the presentation were still an effort, but it was manageable given the work I had put in.

A challenge and something I am proud of was the final presentation. Growing up, I struggled with public speaking and was nervous about having a present for such a long period of time. By rehearsing many times and being passionate about my topic, I was able to speak more naturally about my topic and feel more confident in my abilities. When it came time to present in May 2021, I was able to speak for the whole hour without any notes. Overall, this project taught me a lot about navigating the research process, managing my time, and effectively communicating to audiences.

I worked on a collaborative story writing website powered by blockchain for one of the research labs at Tufts. On the website, anyone can become an author by adding a sentence. Other people can then decide which sentences they want to upvote, and the sentences with the most upvotes then move to the story. Once the story is finished, people can buy the story and all the contributors are listed as authors. The prices of all these actions are very low (around ~$0.1) because the goal of the project is to bring creative minds together on an online platform. This was one of the challenges we faced, since we had to find a network that will allow these cheap prices even with the network gas fee. Initially we wanted to publish on Ethereum Mainnet, but the prices there would be around $10 for just adding a sentence. After researching other networks, we found the much more accessible Polygon Network.

We coded the website in JavaScript and Solidity and it is deployed on the Polygon Network, with MATIC as the cryptocurrency. I worked on this project throughout the whole summer, with no prior experience with blockchain or JavaScript. There were many basics I had to learn and tutorials I had to watch, but I never would have imagined how much I can learn from just one project.

A project I'm truly proud of is my High School Senior Year CS Capstone project. (The CS Capstone project is a year-long project during senior year for students in the Academy for Technology and Computer Science at the Bergen County Academies.) I, along with 2 of my friends, created a Web App titled the BCA Research Hub for our high school.
The BCA Research Hub is an online query tool for BCA Research students to look at previous research projects (titles, materials, & abstracts) for inspiration. A project workflow management tool allows students to follow up with their research advisors on their research progress. BCA students can also upload their project information & documents directly to the MySQL database & Google Drive folder (which all research advisors can access). Thus, the BCA Research Hub is a centralized location for research advisors to access their students' research documents. Lastly, there is a page on the Web App for Research Protocols that can easily be viewed with an in-browser PDF viewer.
We built this project with EJS, JS, Bootstrap, NodeJS + Express, SQL (MySQL relational DB), Railway, Auth0, and Google Drive.
Some challenges I faced were communication and facing "dead ends." My group started using a centralized, easy-to-check messaging system (Discord & Messages) a bit into the project, thus making our early communication efforts difficult. Also, in terms of "dead ends," it would have been beneficial to talk to teachers/ mentors more often before trying something unfamiliar, such as implementing a way for teachers to view students' projects. Lastly, our project had some limitations in the fact that we couldn't disclose confidential project information to the general public, as well as not publicly publishing any unfinished/ in-progress projects.

E3 is a program that allows high school leaders the opportunity to participate in the Mountain View-Los Altos (California) grant-making process, as well as engage with and be mentored by local philanthropists. I was a member of a committee that evaluated each grant application carefully and awarded a total of $10,000 to various regional non-profits. My understanding of nonprofit organizations and my awareness of the value of community service has grown as a result of this experience.

In addition, during my senior year of high school, I participated in the AVID program. This program matches high-achieving upperclassmen tutors with FGLI students. For 2 hours every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, I led group discussions to help my peers deepen their understanding of various subjects.

The project I most want to work on is undoubtedly The Legacy Project. A couple of years ago, my brother and I visited our grandparents' senior center with only our phones and the app "StoryCorps". The purpose of this app is to record and document the past experiences of other individuals in order to preserve their story. We were able to immortalize the stories of 7 seniors, which through the app should eventually be stored in the Library of Congress. Since then, I've been inspired to further this initiative, but have found no other way to do so. The Legacy Project seems like the perfect way for me to continue documenting otherwise lost stories.

If The Legacy Project does not seem the right fit for me, I would love to contribute to any other initiative that will have me.

Last winter I built a customizable VR drum set. The drum set consists of cubes that play an MP3 when hit by the user. There's also a togglable metronome. The user can edit the position and sound of each cube drum. I built the project in Unity and hooked up a VR headset to my laptop to test the program.

One particularly tough challenge was getting drums to only play a sound once when struck. I spent a lot of time researching and troubleshooting with colliders in Unity to fix this issue. Another notable challenge was getting each of the programs I was using to work properly together. I had to tweak many settings options and download a handful of extensions to be able to use VR in Unity.
